Act I

[SCENE I]

Enter the Ghost of Andrea, and with him Revenge.

GHOST

1When this eternal substance of my soul
2Did live imprison’d in my wanton flesh,
3Each in their function serving other’s need,
4I was a courtier in the Spanish court.
5My name was Don Andrea; my descent,
6Though not ignoble, yet inferior far
7To gracious fortunes of my tender youth:
8For there in prime and pride of all my years,
9By duteous service and deserving love,
10In secret I possess’d a worthy dame,
11Which hight sweet Bel-imperia by name.
12But in the harvest of my summer joys
13Death’s winter nipp’d the blossoms of my bliss,
14Forcing divorce betwixt my love and me.
15For in the late conflict with Portingale
16My valour drew me into danger’s mouth
17Till life to death made passage through my wounds.
18When I was slain, my soul descended straight
19To pass the flowing stream of Acheron;
20But churlish Charon, only boatman there,
21Said that, my rites of burial not perform’d,
22I might not sit amongst his passengers.
23Ere Sol had slept three nights in Thetis’ lap
24And slaked his smoking chariot in her flood,
25By Don Horatio, our Knight Marshal’s son,
26My funerals and obsequies were done.
27Then was the ferryman of hell content
28To pass me over to the slimy strand
29That leads to fell Avernus’ ugly waves.
30There, pleasing Cerberus with honey’d speech,
31I pass’d the perils of the foremost porch.
32Not far from hence, amidst ten thousand souls,
33Sat Minos, Aeacus and Rhadamanth,
34To whom no sooner gan I make approach
35To crave a passport for my wandering ghost,
36But Minos’ engraven leaves of lottery
37Drew forth the manner of my life and death.
38‘This knight’, quoth he, ‘both liv’d and died in love,
39And for his love tried fortune of the wars,
40And by war’s fortune lost both love and life’.
41‘Why then’, said Aeacus, ‘convey him hence
42To walk with lovers in our fields of love,
43And spend the course of everlasting time
44Under green myrtle trees and cypress shades’.
45‘No, no’, said Rhadamanth, ‘it were not well
46With loving souls to place a martialist.
47He died in war, and must to martial fields,
48Where wounded Hector lives in lasting pain,
49And Achilles’ Myrmidons do scour the plain’.
50Then Minos, mildest censor of the three,
51Made this device to end the difference:
52‘Send him’, quoth he, ‘to our infernal king
53To doom him as best seems his majesty’.
54To this effect my passport straight was drawn.
55In keeping on my way to Pluto’s court
56Through dreadful shades of ever-glooming night,
57I saw more sights than thousand tongues can tell,
58Or pens can write, or mortal hearts can think.
59Three ways there were. That on the right hand side
60Was ready way unto the foresaid fields
61Where lovers live and bloody martialists,
62But either sort contain’d within his bounds.
63The left hand path, declining fearfully,
64Was ready downfall to the deepest hell,
65Where bloody Furies shakes their whips of steel,
66And poor Ixion turns an endless wheel;
67Where usurers are chok’d with melting gold,
68And wantons are embrac’d with ugly snakes,
69And murderers groan with never-killing wounds,
70And perjur’d wights scalded in boiling lead,
71And all foul sins with torments overwhelm’d.
72’Twixt these two ways I trod the middle path,
73Which brought me to the fair Elysian green,
74In midst whereof there stands a stately tower,
75The walls of brass, the gates of adamant.
76Here finding Pluto with his Proserpine,
77I show’d my passport, humbled on my knee,
78Whereat fair Proserpine began to smile,
79And begg’d that only she might give my doom.
80Pluto was pleas’d and seal’d it with a kiss.
81Forthwith, Revenge, she rounded thee in th’ear,
82And bade thee lead me through the gates of horn,
83Where dreams have passage in the silent night.
84No sooner had she spoke but we were here —
85I wot not how —in twinkling of an eye.

REVENGE

Then know, Andrea, that thou art arriv’d

87Where thou shalt see the author of thy death,
88Don Balthazar, the Prince of Portingale,
89Depriv’d of life by Bel-imperia.
90Here sit we down to see the mystery,
91And serve for chorus in this tragedy.

[SCENE II]

Enter SPANISH KING, GENERAL, CASTILE, and HIERONIMO.

KING

1Now say, Lord General, how fares our camp?

GENERAL

2All well, my sovereign liege, except some few
3That are deceas'd by fortune of the war.

KING

4But what portends thy cheerful countenance
5And posting to our presence thus in haste?
6Speak, man, hath fortune given us victory?

GENERAL

7Victory, my liege, and that with little loss.

KING

8Our Portingales will pay us tribute then?

GENERAL

9Tribute and wonted homage therewithal.

KING

10Then bless'd be heaven and guider of the heavens,
11From whose fair influence such justice flows.

CASTILE

12O multum dilecte Deo, tibi militat aether,
13Et conjuratae curvato poplite gentes
14Succumbunt: recti soror est victoria juris.

KING

15Thanks to my loving brother of Castile.
16But, General, unfold in brief discourse
17Your form of battle and your war’s success,
18That, adding all the pleasure of thy news
19Unto the height of former happiness,
20With deeper wage and greater dignity
21We may reward thy blissful chivalry.

GENERAL

22Where Spain and Portingale do jointly knit
23Their frontiers, leaning on each other’s bound,
24There met our armies in their proud array;
25Both furnish'd well, both full of hope and fear,
26Both menacing alike with daring shows,
27Both vaunting sundry colours of device,
28Both cheerly sounding trumpets, drums and fifes,
29Both raising dreadful clamours to the sky,
30That valleys, hills, and rivers made rebound,
31And heaven itself was frighted with the sound.
32Our battles both were pitch'd in squadron form,
33Each corner strongly fenc'd with wings of shot;
34But ere we join'd and came to push of pike,
35I brought a squadron of our readiest shot
36From out our rearward to begin the fight;
37They brought another wing to encounter us.
38Meanwhile, our ordnance play'd on either side,
39And captains strove to have their valours tried.
40Don Pedro, their chief horsemen’s colonel,
41Did with his cornet bravely make attempt
42To break the order of our battle ranks.
43But Don Rogero, worthy man of war,
44March'd forth against him with our musketeers,
45And stopp'd the malice of his fell approach
46While they maintain hot skirmish too and fro,
47Both battles join and fall to handy blows,
48Their violent shot resembling th’ocean’s rage
49When, roaring loud and with a swelling tide,
50It beats upon the rampiers of huge rocks
51And gapes to swallow neighbour-bounding lands.
52Now while Bellona rageth here and there,
53Thick storms of bullets rain like winter’s hail,
54And shivered lances dark the troubled air.
55Pede pes et cuspide cuspis;
56Arma sonant armis, vir petiturque viro.
57On every side drop captains to the ground,
58And soldiers, some ill-maim’d, some slain outright;
59Here falls a body sundered from his head,
60There legs and arms lie bleeding on the grass,
61Mingled with weapons and unbowell’d steeds
62That, scattering, overspread the purple plain.
63In all this turmoil, three long hours and more
64The victory to neither part inclined,
65Till Don Andrea with his brave lancers
66In their main battle made so great a breach
67That, half dismayed, the multitude retired.
68But Balthazar, the Portingales’ young prince,
69Brought rescue and encouraged them to stay.
70Here-hence the fight was eagerly renewed,
71And in that conflict was Andrea slain,
72Brave man-at-arms, but weak to Balthazar.
73Yet while the Prince, insulting over him,
74Breathed out proud vaunts sounding to our reproach,
75Friendship and hardy valour, joined in one,
76Pricked forth Horatio, our Knight Marshal’s son,
77To challenge forth that Prince in single fight.
78Not long between these twain the fight endured,
79But straight the Prince was beaten from his horse
80And forced to yield him prisoner to his foe.
81When he was taken, all the rest they fled,
82And our carbines pursued them to the death
83Till, Phoebus waning to the western deep,
84Our trumpeters were charged to sound retreat.

KING

85Thanks, good Lord General, for these good news,
86And, for some argument of more to come,
87Take this and wear it for thy sovereign’s sake.

Gives him his chain.

88But tell me now, hast thou confirmed a peace?

GENERAL

89No peace, my liege, but peace conditional,
90That if with homage tribute be well paid,
91The fury of your forces will be stayed.
92And to this peace their Viceroy hath subscribed,

Gives the King a paper.

93And made a solemn vow that during life
94His tribute shall be truly paid to Spain.

KING

95These words, these deeds, become thy person well. —
96But now, Knight Marshal, frolic with thy King,
97For ’tis thy son that wins this battle’s prize.

HIERONIMO

98Long may he live to serve my sovereign liege,
99And soon decay unless he serve my liege.

KING

100Nor thou nor he shall die without reward.

A tucket afar off.

101What means this warning of this trumpet’s sound?

GENERAL

102This tells me that your grace’s men of war,
103Such as war’s fortune hath reserved from death,
104Come marching on towards your royal seat
105To show themselves before your majesty —
106For so I gave in charge at my depart —
107Whereby by demonstration shall appear
108That all, except three hundred or few more,
109Are safe returned and by their foes enriched.

The army enters; BALTHAZAR, between LORENZO and HORATIO, captive.

KING

110A gladsome sight! I long to see them here!

They enter and pass by.

111Was that the warlike Prince of Portingale,
112That by our nephew was in triumph led?

GENERAL

113It was, my liege, the Prince of Portingale.

KING

114But what was he that on the other side
115Held him by th’ arm as partner of the prize?

HIERONIMO

116That was my son, my gracious sovereign,
117Of whom though from his tender infancy
118My loving thoughts did never hope but well,
119He never pleas’d his father’s eyes till now,
120Nor fill’d my heart with over-cloying joys.

KING

121Go, let them march once more about these walls,
122That, staying them, we may confer and talk
123With our brave prisoner and his double guard.
124Hieronimo, it greatly pleaseth us
125That in our victory thou have a share
126By virtue of thy worthy son’s exploit.

Enter again.

127Bring hither the young Prince of Portingale:
128The rest march on, but ere they be dismiss’d,
129We will bestow on every soldier
130Two ducats, and on every leader ten,
131That they may know our largess welcomes them.

Exeunt all [the army] but Balthazar, Lorenzo, and Horatio.

132Welcome, Don Balthazar; welcome, nephew;
133And thou, Horatio, thou art welcome too.
134Young Prince, although thy father’s hard misdeeds
135In keeping back the tribute that he owes
136Deserve but evil measure at our hands,
137Yet shalt thou know that Spain is honourable.

BALTHAZAR

138The trespass that my father made in peace
139Is now controll’d by fortune of the wars;
140And cards once dealt, it boots not ask why so.
141His men are slain, a weakening to his realm;
142His colours seiz’d, a blot unto his name;
143His son distress’d, a corsive to his heart:
144These punishments may clear his late offence.

KING

145Ay, Balthazar, if he observe this truce,
146Our peace will grow the stronger for these wars.
147Meanwhile, live thou, though not in liberty,
148Yet free from bearing any servile yoke;
149For, in our hearing, thy deserts were great,
150And, in our sight, thyself art gracious.

BALTHAZAR

151And I shall study to deserve this grace.

KING

152But tell me, —for their holding makes me doubt—
153To which of these twain art thou prisoner?

LORENZO

154To me, my liege.

HORATIO

To me, my liege. To me, my sovereign.

LORENZO

155This hand first took his courser by the reins.

HORATIO

156But first my lance did put him from his horse.

LORENZO

157I seiz’d his weapon and enjoy’d it first.

HORATIO

158But first I forc’d him lay his weapons down.

KING

159Let go his arm, upon our privilege.

Let him go.

160Say, worthy Prince, to whether did’st thou yield?

BALTHAZAR

161To him in courtesy, to this perforce:
162He spake me fair, this other gave me strokes;
163He promis’d life, this other threaten’d death;
164He won my love, this other conquer’d me;
165And truth to say, I yield myself to both.

HIERONIMO

166But that I know your grace for just and wise,
167And might seem partial in this difference,
168Enforc’d by nature and by law of arms
169My tongue should plead for young Horatio’s right.
170He hunted well that was a lion’s death,
171Not he that in a garment wore his skin;
172So hares may pull dead lions by the beard.

KING

173Content thee, Marshal, thou shalt have no wrong,
174And, for thy sake, thy son shall want no right.
175Will both abide the censure of my doom?

LORENZO

176I crave no better than your grace awards.

HORATIO

177Nor I, although I sit beside my right.

KING

178Then by my judgement, thus your strife shall end:
179You both deserve and both shall have reward.
180Nephew, thou took’st his weapon and his horse:
181His weapons and his horse are thy reward.
182Horatio, thou did’st force him first to yield:
183His ransom therefore is thy valour’s fee;
184Appoint the sum as you shall both agree.
185But, nephew, thou shalt have the Prince in guard,
186For thine estate best fitteth such a guest:
187Horatio’s house were small for all his train.
188Yet, in regard thy substance passeth his,
189And that just guerdon may befall desert,
190To him we yield the armour of the Prince.
191How likes Don Balthazar of this device?

BALTHAZAR

192Right well, my liege, if this provison were,
193That Don Horatio bear us company,
194Whom I admire and love for chivalry.

KING

195Horatio, leave him not that loves thee so.
196Now let us hence to see our soldiers paid,
197And feast our prisoner as our friendly guest.

Exeunt.

[SCENE III]

Enter VICEROY, ALEXANDRO, VILLUPPO [and Attendants].

VICEROY

1Is our Ambassador dispatch’d for Spain?

ALEXANDRO

2Two days, my liege, are pass’d since his depart.

VICEROY

3And tribute-payment gone along with him?

ALEXANDRO

4Ay, my good lord.

VICEROY

5Then rest we here awhile in our unrest,
6And feed our sorrows with some inward sighs,
7For deepest cares break never into tears.
8But wherefore sit I in a regal throne?
9This better fits a wretch’s endless moan.

Falls to the ground.

10Yet this is higher than my fortunes reach,
11And therefore better than my state deserves.
12Ay, ay, this earth, image of melancholy,
13Seeks him whom fates adjudge to misery.
14Here let me lie; now am I at the lowest.
15Qui jacet in terra, non habet unde cadat.
16In me consumpsit vires fortuna nocendo:
17Nil superest ut jam possit obesse magis.
18Yes, Fortune may bereave me of my crown:
19Here, take it now; — let Fortune do her worst,
20She will not rob me of this sable weed:
21O no, she envies none but pleasant things.
22Such is the folly of despiteful chance!
23Fortune is blind, and sees not my deserts;
24So is she deaf, and hears not my laments;
25And could she hear, yet is she wilful mad,
26And therefore will not pity my distress.
27Suppose that she could pity me, what then?
28What help can be expected at her hands
29Whose foot is standing on a rolling stone,
30And mind more mutable than fickle winds?
31Why wail I then, where’s hope of no redress?
32O yes, complaining makes my grief seem less.
33My late ambition hath distain’d my faith,
34My breach of faith occasion’d bloody wars,
35Those bloody wars have spent my treasure,
36And with my treasure my people’s blood,
37And with their blood, my joy and best belov’d,
38My best belov’d, my sweet and only son.
39Oh, wherefore went I not to war myself?
40The cause was mine; I might have died for both:
41My years were mellow, his but young and green;
42My death were natural, but his was forc’d.

ALEXANDRO

43No doubt, my liege, but still the Prince survives.

VICEROY

44Survives! ay, where?

ALEXANDRO

45In Spain, a prisoner by mischance of war.

VICEROY

46Then they have slain him for his father’s fault.

ALEXANDRO

47That were a breach to common law of arms.

VICEROY

48They reck no laws that meditate revenge.

ALEXANDRO

49His ransom’s worth will stay from foul revenge.

VICEROY

50No, if he liv’d the news would soon be here.

ALEXANDRO

51Nay, evil news fly faster still than good.

VICEROY

52Tell me no more of news, for he is dead.

VILLUPPO

53My sovereign, pardon the author of ill news,
54And I’ll bewray the fortune of thy son.

VICEROY

55Speak on, I’ll guerdon thee whate’er it be:
56Mine ear is ready to receive ill news,
57My heart grown hard ’gainst mischief’s battery.
58Stand up, I say, and tell thy tale at large.

VILLUPPO

59[Rises.] Then hear that truth which these mine eyes have seen:
60When both the armies were in battle join’d,
61Don Balthazar, amidst the thickest troops,
62To win renown, did wondrous feats of arms:
63Amongst the rest I saw him hand to hand
64In single fight with their Lord general;
65Till Alexandro, that here counterfeits
66Under the colour of a duteous friend,
67Discharg’d his pistol at the Prince’s back,
68As though he would have slain their general:
69But therewithal Don Balthazar fell down;
70And when he fell, then we began to fly:
71But had he liv’d, the day had sure been ours.

ALEXANDRO

72O wicked forgery! O traitorous miscreant!

VICEROY

73Hold thou thy peace! But now, Villuppo, say,
74Where then became the carcase of my son?

VILLUPPO

75I saw them drag it to the Spanish tents.

VICEROY

76Ay, ay, my nightly dreams have told me this. —
77Thou false, unkind, unthankful traitorous beast,
78Wherein had Balthazar offended thee
79That thou shouldst thus betray him to our foes?
80Was’t Spanish gold that bleared so thine eyes
81That thou couldst see no part of our deserts?
82Perchance because thou art Terceira’s lord,
83Thou hadst some hope to wear this diadem,
84If first my son and then myself were slain;
85But thy ambitious thought shall break thy neck.
86Ay, this was it that made thee spill his blood:

Takes the crown and puts it on again.

87But I’ll now wear it till thy blood be spilt.

ALEXANDRO

88Vouchsafe, dread sovereign, to hear me speak.

VICEROY

89Away with him; his sight is second hell.
90Keep him till we determine of his death.

[Exit Alexandro, guarded.]

91If Balthazar be dead, he shall not live.
92Villuppo, follow us for thy reward.

Exit Viceroy.

VILLUPPO

93Thus have I with an envious, forged tale
94Deceiv’d the King, betray’d mine enemy,
95And hope for guerdon of my villainy.

Exit.

[SCENE IV]

Enter HORATIO and BEL-IMPERIA.

BEL-IMPERIA

1Signor Horatio, this is the place and hour
2Wherein I must entreat thee to relate
3The circumstance of Don Andrea’s death,
4Who, living, was my garland’s sweetest flower,
5And in his death hath buried my delights.

HORATIO

6For love of him and service to yourself,
7I nill refuse this heavy doleful charge;
8Yet tears and sighs, I fear, will hinder me.
9When both our armies were enjoin’d in fight,
10Your worthy chevalier amidst the thick’st,
11For glorious cause still aiming at the fairest,
12Was at the last by young Don Balthazar
13Encounter’d hand to hand: Their fight was long,
14Their hearts were great, their clamours menacing,
15Their strength alike, their strokes both dangerous.
16But wrathful Nemesis, that wicked power,
17Envying at Andrea’s praise and worth,
18Cut short his life to end his praise and worth.
19She, she herself, disguis’d in armour’s mask —
20As Pallas was before proud Pergamus —
21Brought in a fresh supply of halberdiers,
22Which paunch’d his horse and ding’d him to the ground.
23Then young Don Balthazar with ruthless rage,
24Taking advantage of his foe’s distress,
25Did finish what his halberdiers begun,
26And left not, till Andrea’s life was done.
27Then, though too late, incens’d with just remorse,
28I with my band set forth against the prince,
29And brought him prisoner from his halberdiers.

BEL-IMPERIA

30Would thou hadst slain him that so slew my love!
31But then was Don Andrea’s carcase lost?

HORATIO

32No, that was it for which I chiefly strove,
33Nor stepp’d I back till I recover’d him:
34I took him up, and wound him in mine arms,
35And, wielding him unto my private tent,
36There laid him down, and dew’d him with my tears,
37And sigh’d and sorrow’d as became a friend.
38But neither friendly sorrow, sighs, nor tears
39Could win pale death from his usurpèd right.
40Yet this I did, and less I could not do:
41I saw him honour’d with due funeral.
42This scarf I pluck’d from off his lifeless arm,
43And wear it in remembrance of my friend.

BEL-IMPERIA

44I know the scarf: would he had kept it still;
45For, had he liv’d, he would have kept it still,
46And worn it for his Bel-imperia’s sake:
47For ’twas my favour at his last depart.
48But now wear thou it both for him and me;
49For, after him, thou hast deserv’d it best.
50But, for thy kindness in his life and death,
51Be sure, while Bel-imperia’s life endures,
52She will be Don Horatio’s thankful friend.

HORATIO

53And, madam, Don Horatio will not slack
54Humbly to serve fair Bel-imperia.
55But now, if your good liking stand thereto,
56I’ll crave your pardon to go seek the prince;
57For so the Duke, your father, gave me charge.Exit.

BEL-IMPERIA

58Ay, go, Horatio, leave me here alone;
59For solitude best fits my cheerless mood.
60Yet what avails to wail Andrea’s death,
61From whence Horatio proves my second love?
62Had he not lov’d Andrea as he did,
63He could not sit in Bel-imperia’s thoughts.
64But how can love find harbour in my breast,
65Till I revenge the death of my belov’d?
66Yes, second love shall further my revenge.
67I’ll love Horatio, my Andrea’s friend,
68The more to spite the Prince that wrought his end;
69And where Don Balthazar, that slew my love,
70Himself now pleads for favour at my hands,
71He shall, in rigour of my just disdain,
72Reap long repentance for his murderous deed.
73For what was’t else but murderous cowardice,
74So many to oppress one valiant knight,
75Without respect of honour in the fight?
76And here he comes that murder’d my delight.

Enter LORENZO and BALTHAZAR.

LORENZO

77Sister, what means this melancholy walk?

BEL-IMPERIA

78That for a while I wish no company.

LORENZO

79But here the Prince is come to visit you.

BEL-IMPERIA

80That argues that he lives in liberty.

BALTHAZAR

81No, madam, but in pleasing servitude.

BEL-IMPERIA

82Your prison then belike is your conceit.

BALTHAZAR

83Ay, by conceit my freedom is enthrall’d.

BEL-IMPERIA

84Then with conceit enlarge yourself again.

BALTHAZAR

85What if conceit have laid my heart to gage?

BEL-IMPERIA

86Pay that you borrow’d and recover it.

BALTHAZAR

87I die, if it return from whence it lies.

BEL-IMPERIA

88A heartless man, and live? A miracle!

BALTHAZAR

89Ay, lady, love can work such miracles.

LORENZO

90Tush, tush, my lord! let go these ambages,
91And in plain terms acquaint her with your love.

BEL-IMPERIA

92What boots complaint when there’s no remedy?

BALTHAZAR

93Yes, to your gracious self must I complain,
94In whose fair answer lies my remedy,
95On whose perfection all my thoughts attend,
96In whose aspect mine eyes find beauty’s bower,
97In whose translucent breast my heart is lodg’d.

BEL-IMPERIA

98Alas, my lord, these are but words of course,
99And but devise to drive me from this place.

She, in going in, lets fall her glove, which Horatio, coming out, takes up.

HORATIO

100Madam, your glove.

BEL-IMPERIA

101Thanks, good Horatio; take it for thy pains.

BALTHAZAR

102Signior Horatio stoop’d in happy time.

HORATIO

103I reap’d more grace than I deserv’d or hop’d.

LORENZO

104My lord, be not dismay’d for what is past:
105You know that women oft are humorous;
106These clouds will overblow with little wind;
107Let me alone, I’ll scatter them myself.
108Meanwhile let us devise to spend the time
109In some delightful sports and revelling.

HORATIO

110The King, my lords, is coming hither straight
111To feast the Portingale ambassador;
112Things were in readiness before I came.

BALTHAZAR

113Then here it fits us to attend the King,
114To welcome hither our ambassador,
115And learn my father and my country’s health.

Enter the Banquet, Trumpets, the KING and Ambassador.

KING

116See, lord Ambassador, how Spain entreats
117Their prisoner Balthazar, thy Viceroy’s son:
118We pleasure more in kindness than in wars.

AMBASSADOR

119Sad is our King, and Portingale laments,
120Supposing that Don Balthazar is slain.

BALTHAZAR

121[aside.] So am I slain, by beauty’s tyranny. —aparte
122You see, my lord, how Balthazar is slain:
123I frolic with the Duke of Castile’s son,
124Wrapp’d every hour in pleasures of the court,
125And grac’d with favours of his majesty.

KING

126Put off your greetings till our feast be done.
127Now come and sit with us, and taste our cheer.

Sit to the banquet.

128Sit down, young Prince, you are our second guest;
129Brother, sit down; and, nephew, take your place.
130Signior Horatio, wait thou upon our cup,
131For well thou hast deserved to be honour’d.
132Now, lordings, fall to. Spain is Portugal,
133And Portugal is Spain; we both are friends,
134Tribute is paid, and we enjoy our right.
135But where is old Hieronimo, our Marshal?
136He promis’d us in honour of our guest,
137To grace our banquet with some pompous jest.

Enter HIERONIMO, with a Drum, three Knights, each [hangs up] his scutcheon; Then he fetches three Kings, they take their crowns and them captive.

138Hieronimo, this masque contents mine eye,
139Although I sound not well the mystery.

HIERONIMO

140The first arm’d knight that hung his scutcheon up,

He takes the scutcheon and gives it to the King.

141Was English Robert, Earl of Gloucester,
142Who, when King Stephen bore sway in Albion,
143Arriv’d with five and twenty thousand men
144In Portingale and by success of war
145Enforc’d the king, then but a Saracen,
146To bear the yoke of the English monarchy.

KING

147My lord of Portingale, by this you see
148That which may comfort both your King and you,
149And make your late discomfort seem the less.
150But say, Hieronimo, what was the next?

HIERONIMO

151The second knight that hung his scutcheon up

He doth as he did before.

152Was Edmund, Earl of Kent in Albion,
153When English Richard wore the diadem.
154He came likewise and razed Lisbon walls,
155And took the king of Portingale in fight;
156For which, and other such-like service done,
157He after was created Duke of York.

KING

158This is another special argument
159That Portingale may deign to bear our yoke,
160When it by little England hath been yok’d.
161But now, Hieronimo, what were the last?

HIERONIMO

162The third and last, not least in our account,

Doing as before

163Was, as the rest, a valiant Englishman,
164Brave John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster,
165As by his scutcheon plainly may appear.
166He with a puissant army came to Spain,
167And took our King of Castile prisoner.

AMBASSADOR

168This is an argument for our Viceroy
169That Spain may not insult for her success,
170Since English warriors likewise conquer’d Spain
171And made them bow their knees to Albion.

KING

172Hieronimo, I drink to thee for this device,
173Which hath pleas’d both the ambassador and me:
174Pledge me, Hieronimo, if thou love thy King.

Takes the cup of Horatio.

175My lord, I fear we sit but over-long,
176Unless our dainties were more delicate;
177But welcome are you to the best we have.
178Now let us in, that you may be dispatch’d:
179I think our council is already set.

Exeunt omnes.

[SCENE V]

Ghost of Andrea, Revenge.

ANDREA

1Come we for this from depth of underground,
2To see him feast that gave me my death’s wound?
3These pleasant sights are sorrow to my soul:
4Nothing but league, and love, and banqueting?

REVENGE

5Be still, Andrea; ere we go from hence,
6I’ll turn their friendship into fell despite,
7Their love to mortal hate, their day to night,
8Their hope into despair, their peace to war,
9Their joys to pain, their bliss to misery.

Act II

[SCENE I]

Enter LORENZO and BALTHAZAR.

LORENZO

1My lord, though Bel-imperia seem thus coy,
2Let reason hold you in your wonted joy:
3In time the savage bull sustains the yoke,
4In time all haggard hawks will stoop to lure,
5In time small wedges cleave the hardest oak,
6In time the flint is pierc’d with softest shower,
7And she in time will fall from her disdain,
8And rue the suff’rance of your friendly pain.

BALTHAZAR

9No, she is wilder and more hard withal.
10Than beast, or bird, or tree, or stony wall.
11But wherefore blot I Bel-imperia’s name?
12It is my fault, not she, that merits blame.
13My feature is not to content her sight,
14My words are rude and work her no delight.
15The lines I send her are but harsh and ill,
16Such as do drop from Pan and Marsyas’ quill.
17My presents are not of sufficient cost,
18And being worthless, all my labour’s lost.
19Yet might she love me for my valiancy:
20Ay, but that’s slandered by captivity.
21Yet might she love me to content her sire:
22Ay, but her reason masters his desire.
23Yet might she love me as her brother’s friend:
24Ay, but her hopes aim at some other end.
25Yet might she love me to uprear her state:
26Ay, but perhaps she hopes some nobler mate.
27Yet might she love me as her beauty’s thrall:
28Ay, but I fear she cannot love at all.

LORENZO

29My lord, for my sake, leave these ecstasies,
30And doubt not but we’ll find some remedy.
31Some cause there is that lets you not be lov’d;
32First that must needs be known and then remov’d.
33What if my sister love some other knight?

BALTHAZAR

34My summer’s day will turn to winter’s night.

LORENZO

35I have already found a stratagem,
36To sound the bottom of this doubtful theme.
37My lord, for once you shall be rul’d by me;
38Hinder me not, whate’er you hear or see.
39By force or fair means will I cast about
40To find the truth of all this question out.
41Ho, Pedringano!

PEDRINGANO

42Signior!

LORENZO

43Vien qui presto.

Enter PEDRINGANO.

PEDRINGANO

44Hath your lordship any service to command me?

LORENZO

45Ay, Pedringano, service of import;
46And, not to spend the time in trifling words,
47Thus stands the case: it is not long, thou know’st,
48Since I did shield thee from my father’s wrath,
49For thy conveyance in Andrea’s love,
50For which thou wert adjudg’d to punishment:
51I stood betwixt thee and thy punishment,
52And since, thou know’st how I have favour’d thee.
53Now to these favours will I add reward,
54Not with fair words, but store of golden coin,
55And lands and living join’d with dignities,
56If thou but satisfy my just demand:
57Tell truth and have me for thy lasting friend.

PEDRINGANO

58Whate’er it be your lordship shall demand,
59My bounden duty bids me tell the truth.
60If case it lie in me to tell the truth.

LORENZO

61Then, Pedringano, this is my demand:
62Whom loves my sister Bel-imperia?
63For she reposeth all her trust in thee.
64Speak, man, and gain both friendship and reward:
65I mean, whom loves she in Andrea’s place?

PEDRINGANO

66Alas, my lord, since Don Andrea’s death
67I have no credit with her as before;
68And therefore know not if she love or no.

LORENZO

69Nay, if thou dally, then I am thy foe,

<sup> Q4 </sup> [Draws his sword.] </sup> Q4 <sup>

70And fear shall force what friendship cannot win:
71Thy death shall bury what thy life conceals;
72Thou diest for more esteeming her than me.

PEDRINGANO

73Oh, stay, my lord!

LORENZO

74Yet speak the truth and I will guerdon thee,
75And shield thee from whatever can ensue,
76And will conceal whate’er proceeds from thee.
77But if thou dally once again, thou diest.

PEDRINGANO

78If Madam Bel-imperia be in love —

LORENZO

79What, villain! ifs and ands?

<sup> Q4 </sup> [Offers to kill him.] </sup> Q4 <sup>

PEDRINGANO

80Oh, stay, my lord! She loves Horatio.

Balthazar starts back.

LORENZO

81What? Don Horatio, our Knight Marshal’s son?

PEDRINGANO

82Even him, my lord.

LORENZO

83Now say but how tohu know’st he is her love,
84And thou shalt find me kind and liberal:
85Stand up, I say, and fearless tell the truth.

PEDRINGANO

86She sent him letters, which myself perus’d,
87Full-fraught with lines and arguments of love,
88Preferring him before Prince Balthazar.

LORENZO

89Swear on this cross that what thou say’st is true,
90And that thou wilt conceal what thou hast told.

PEDRINGANO

91I swear to both, by him that made us all.

LORENZO

92In hope thine oath is true, here’s thy reward:
93But if I prove thee perjur’d and unjust,
94This very sword whereon thou took’st thine oath,
95Shall be the worker of thy tragedy.

PEDRINGANO

96What I have said is true, and shall, for me,
97Be still conceal’d from Bel-imperia.
98Besides, your honour’s liberality
99Deserves my duteous service, even till death.

LORENZO

100Let this be all that thou shalt do for me:
101Be watchful when and where these lovers meet,
102And give me notice in some secret sort.

PEDRINGANO

103I will, my lord.

LORENZO

104Then shalt thou find that I am liberal.
105Thou know’st that I can more advance thy state
106Than she; be therefore wise and fail me not.
107Go and attend her as thy custom is,
108Lest absence make her think thou dost amiss.

Exit Pedringano.

109Why so, tam armis quam ingenio:
110Where words prevail not, violence prevails;
111But gold doth more than either of them both.
112How likes Prince Balthazar this stratagem?

BALTHAZAR

113Both well and ill; it makes me glad and sad:
114Glad, that I know the hinderer of my love;
115Sad, that I fear she hates me whom I love.
116Glad, that I know on whom to be reveng’d;
117Sad, that she’ll fly me if I take revenge.
118Yet must I take revenge or die myself,
119For love resisted grows impatient.
120I think Horatio be my destin’d plague:
121First in his hand he brandished a sword,
122And with that sword he fiercely waged war,
123And in that war he gave me dangerous wounds,
124And by those wounds he forced me to yield,
125And by my yielding I became his slave.
126Now in his mouth he carries pleasing words,
127Which pleasing words do harbour sweet conceits,
128Which sweet conceits are lim’d with sly deceits,
129Which sly deceits smooth Bel-imperia’s ears,
130And through her ears dive down into her heart,
131And in her heart set him where I should stand.
132Thus hath he ta’en my body by his force,
133And now by sleight would captivate my soul:
134But in his fall I’ll tempt the destinies,
135And either lose my life, or win my love.

LORENZO

136Let’s go, my lord; your staying stays revenge.
137Do you but follow me, and gain your love:
138Her favour must be won by his remove.

Exeunt.

[SCENE II]

Enter HORATIO and BEL-IMPERIA.

HORATIO

1Now, madam, since by favour of your love
2Our hidden smoke is turn’d to open flame,
3And that with looks and words we feed our thoughts
4(Two chief contents, where more cannot be had),
5Thus, in the midst of love’s fair blandishments,
6Why show you sign of inward languishments?

PEDRINGANO showeth all to the Prince and LORENZO, placing them in secret [above].

BEL-IMPERIA

7My heart, sweet friend, is like a ship at sea:
8She wisheth port, where, riding all at ease,
9She may repair what stormy times have worn,
10And leaning on the shore, may sing with joy
11That pleasure follows pain, and bliss annoy.
12Possession of thy love is th’ only port
13Wherein my heart, with fears and hopes long toss’d,
14Each hour doth wish and long to make resort,
15There to repair the joys that it hath lost,
16And, sitting safe, to sing in Cupid’s quire
17That sweetest bliss is crown of love’s desire.

BALTHAZAR above.

BALTHAZAR

18O sleep, mine eyes, see not my love profan’d;
19Be deaf, my ears, hear not my discontent;
20Die, heart: another joys what thou deserv’st.

LORENZO

21Watch still, mine eyes, to see this love disjoin’d;
22Hear still, mine ears, to hear them both lament;
23Live, heart, to joy at fond Horatio’s fall.

BEL-IMPERIA

24Why stands Horatio speechless all this while?

HORATIO

25The less I speak, the more I meditate.

BEL-IMPERIA

26But whereon dost thou chiefly meditate?

HORATIO

27On dangers past, and pleasures to ensue.

BALTHAZAR

28On pleasures past, and dangers to ensue.

BEL-IMPERIA

29What dangers and what pleasures dost thou mean?

HORATIO

30Dangers of war, and pleasures of our love.

LORENZO

31Dangers of death, but pleasures none at all.

BEL-IMPERIA

32Let dangers go, thy war shall be with me:
33But such a war as breaks no bond of peace.
34Speak thou fair words, I’ll cross them with fair words;
35Send thou sweet looks, I’ll meet them with sweet looks;
36Write loving lines, I’ll answer loving lines;
37Give me a kiss, I’ll countercheck thy kiss:
38Be this our warring peace, or peaceful war.

HORATIO

39But, gracious madam, then appoint the field,
40Where trial of this war shall first be made.

BALTHAZAR

41Ambitious villain, how his boldness grows!

BEL-IMPERIA

42Then be thy father’s pleasant bower the field,
43Where first we vow’d a mutual amity;
44The court were dangerous; that place is safe.
45Our hour shall be when Vesper ‘gins to rise,
46That summons home distressful travellers:
47There none shall hear us but the harmless birds;
48Haply the gentle nightingale
49Shall carol us asleep ere we be ware,
50And, singing with the prickle at her breast,
51Tell our delight and mirthful dalliance.
52Till then each hour will seem a year and more.

HORATIO

53But, honey sweet and honourable love,
54Return we now into your father’s sight:
55Dangerous suspicion waits on our delight.

LORENZO

56Ay, danger mixed with jealous despite
57Shall send thy soul into eternal night.

Exeunt.

[SCENE III]

Enter KING OF SPAIN, Portingale Ambassador, DON CYPRIAN, etc.

KING

1Brother of Castile, to the Prince’s love
2What says your daughter Bel-imperia?

CYPRIAN

3Although she coy it as becomes her kind,
4And yet dissemble that she loves the prince,
5I doubt not, I, but she will stoop in time.
6And were she froward, which she will not be,
7Yet herein shall she follow my advice,
8Which is to love him or forgo my love.

KING

9Then, lord Ambassador of Portingale,
10Advise thy King to make this marriage up,
11For strengthening of our late-confirmed league;
12I know no better means to make us friends.
13Her dowry shall be large and liberal:
14Besides that she is daughter and half-heir
15Unto our brother here, Don Cyprian,
16And shall enjoy the moiety of his land,
17I’ll grace her marriage with an uncle’s gift,
18And this it is: in case the match go forward,
19The tribute which you pay shall be releas’d,
20And if by Balthazar she have a son,
21He shall enjoy the kingdom after us.

AMBASSADOR

22I’ll make the motion to my sovereign liege,
23And work it, if my counsel may prevail.

KING

24Do so, my lord, and, if he give consent,
25I hope his presence here will honour us,
26In celebration of the nuptial day;
27And let himself determine of the time.

AMBASSADOR

28Will’t please your grace command me ought beside?

KING

29Commend me to the King, and so farewell.
30But where’s Prince Balthazar to take his leave?

AMBASSADOR

31That is perform’d already, my good lord.

KING

32Amongst the rest of what you have in charge,
33The prince’s ransom must not be forgot:
34That’s none of mine, but his that took him prisoner,
35And well his forwardness deserves reward:
36It was Horatio, our Knight Marshal’s son.

AMBASSADOR

37Between us there’s a price already pitch’d,
38And shall be sent with all convenient speed.

KING

39Then once again farewell, my lord.

AMBASSADOR

40Farewell, my lord of Castile and the rest.

Exit.

KING

41Now, brother, you must take some little pains
42To win fair Bel-imperia from her will:
43Young virgins must be ruled by their friends.
44The prince is amiable and loves her well;
45If she neglect him and forgo his love,
46She both will wrong her own estate and ours.
47Therefore, whiles I do entertain the prince
48With greatest pleasure that our court affords,
49Endeavour you to win your daughter’s thought:
50If she give back, all this will come to naught.

Exeunt.

[SCENE IV]

Enter HORATIO, BEL-IMPERIA, and PEDRINGANO.

HORATIO

1Now that the night begins with sable wings
2To overcloud the brightness of the sun,
3And that in darkness pleasures may be done,
4Come, Bel-imperia, let us to the bower,
5And there in safety pass a pleasant hour.

BEL-IMPERIA

6I follow thee, my love, and will not back,
7Although my fainting heart controls my soul.

HORATIO

8Why, make you doubt of Pedringano’s faith?

BEL-IMPERIA

9No, he is as trusty as my second self. —
10Go, Pedringano, watch without the gate,
11And let us know if any make approach.

PEDRINGANO

12[aside.] Instead of watching, I’ll deserve more goldaparte
13By fetching Don Lorenzo to this match.

Exit Pedringano.

HORATIO

14What means my love?

BEL-IMPERIA

What means my love? I know not what myself;
15And yet my heart foretells me some mischance.

HORATIO

16Sweet, say not so; fair fortune is our friend,
17And heavens have shut up day to pleasure us.
18The stars, thou see’st, hold back their twinkling shine,
19And Luna hides herself to pleasure us.

BEL-IMPERIA

20Thou hast prevail’d; I’ll conquer my misdoubt,
21And in thy love and counsel drown my fear.
22I fear no more; love now is all my thoughts.
23Why sit we not? for pleasure asketh ease.

HORATIO

24The more thou sitt’st within these leavy bowers,
25The more will Flora deck it with her flowers.

BEL-IMPERIA

26Ay, but if Flora spy Horatio here,
27Her jealous eye will think I sit too near.

HORATIO

28Hark, madam, how the birds record by night,
29For joy that Bel-imperia sits in sight.

BEL-IMPERIA

30No, Cupid counterfeits the nightingale,
31To frame sweet music to Horatio’s tale.

HORATIO

32If Cupid sing, then Venus is not far:
33Ay, thou art Venus, or some fairer star.

BEL-IMPERIA

34If I be Venus, thou must needs be Mars;
35And where Mars reigneth, there must needs be wars.

HORATIO

36Then thus begin our wars: put forth thy hand,
37That it may combat with my ruder hand.

BEL-IMPERIA

38Set forth thy foot to try the push of mine.

HORATIO

39But first my looks shall combat against thine.

BEL-IMPERIA

40Then ward thyself: I dart this kiss at thee.

HORATIO

41Thus I retort the dart thou threw’st at me.

BEL-IMPERIA

42Nay then, to gain the glory of the field,
43My twining arms shall yoke and make thee yield.

HORATIO

44Nay, then, my arms are large and strong withal:
45Thus elms by vines are compass’d till they fall.

BEL-IMPERIA

46O, let me go; for in my troubled eyes
47Now may’st thou read that life in passion dies.

HORATIO

48O, stay a while, and I will die with thee;
49So shalt thou yield, and yet have conquer’d me.

BEL-IMPERIA

50Who’s there? Pedringano! we are betray’d!

Enter LORENZO, BALTHAZAR, SERBERINE, PEDRINGANO, disguised.

LORENZO

51My lord, away with her, take her aside. —
52O sir, forbear: your valour is already tried.
53Quickly dispatch, my masters.

They hang him in the arbour.

HORATIO

54What, will you murder me?

LORENZO

55Ay, thus, and thus: these are the fruits of love.

They stab him.

BEL-IMPERIA

56O, save his life, and let me die for him!
57O, save him, brother, Save him, Balthazar:
58I lov’d Horatio, but he lov’d not me.

BALTHAZAR

59But Balthazar loves Bel-imperia.

LORENZO

60Although his life were still ambitious-proud,
61Yet is he at the highest now he is dead.

BEL-IMPERIA

62Murder! Murder! Help, Hieronimo, help!

LORENZO

63Come, stop her mouth, away with her.

Exeunt [leaving Horatio’s body].

Enter HIERONIMO in his shirt, etc.

HIERONIMO

64What outcries pluck me from my naked bed,
65And chill my throbbing heart with trembling fear,
66Which never danger yet could daunt before?
67Who calls Hieronimo? Speak, here I am.
68I did not slumber, therefore ’twas no dream.
69No, no, it was some woman cried for help,
70And there within this garden did she cry,
71And in this garden must I rescue her. —
72But stay, what murd’rous spectacle is this?
73A man hang’d up, and all the murderers gone!
74And in my bower, to lay the guilt on me!
75This place was made for pleasure, not for death.

He cuts him down.

76Those garments that he wears I oft have seen.—
77Alas, it is Horatio, my sweet son!
78O no, but he that whilom was my son!
79O, was it thou that call’dst me from my bed?
80O speak, if any spark of life remain:
81I am thy father; who hath slain my son?
82What savage monster, not of human kind,
83Hath here been glutted with thy harmless blood,
84And left thy bloody corpse dishonour’d here,
85For me, amidst these dark and deathful shades,
86To drown thee with an ocean of my tears?
87O heavens, why made you night to cover sin?
88By day this deed of darkness had not been.
89O earth, why didst thou not in time devour
90The vild profaner of this sacred bower?
91O poor Horatio, what hadst thou misdone,
92To leese thy life, ere life was new begun?
93O wicked butcher, whatsoe’er thou wert,
94How could thou strangle virtue and desert?
95Ay me most wretched, that have lost my joy,
96In leesing my Horatio, my sweet boy!

Enter ISABELLA.

ISABELLA

97My husband’s absence makes my heart to throb. —
98Hieronimo!

HIERONIMO

99Here, Isabella, help me to lament;
100For sighs are stopp’d and all my tears are spent.

ISABELLA

101What world of grief — My son Horatio!
102O, where’s the author of this endless woe?

HIERONIMO

103To know the author were some ease of grief;
104For in revenge my heart would find relief.

ISABELLA

105Then is he gone? And is my son gone too?
106O, gush out, tears, fountains and floods of tears;
107Blow, sighs, and raise an everlasting storm;
108For outrage fits our cursed wretchedness.
109<sup> Q4 </sup> Ay me, Hieronimo, sweet husband, speak!

HIERONIMO

110He supp’d with us to-night, frolic and merry,
111And said he would go visit Balthazar
112At the Duke’s palace: there the Prince doth lodge.
113He had no custom to stay out so late;
114He may be in his chamber; Some go see.
115Rodorigo, ho!

Enter PEDRO and JAQUES.

ISABELLA

116Ay me, he raves! Sweet Hieronimo!

HIERONIMO

117True, all Spain takes note of it.
118Besides, he is so generally belov’d;
119His majesty the other day did grace him
120With waiting on his cup: these be favours,
121Which do assure he cannot be short-liv’d.

ISABELLA

122Sweet Hieronimo!

HIERONIMO

123I wonder how this fellow got his clothes!
124Sirrah, sirrah, I’ll know the truth of all:
125Jaques, run to the Duke of Castile’s presently,
126And bid my son Horatio to come home:
127I and his mother have had strange dreams to-night.
128Do ye hear me, sir?

JAQUES

Do ye hear me, sir? Ay, sir.

HIERONIMO

Do ye hear me, sir? Ay, sir. Well, sir, begone.
129Pedro, come hither; Know’st thou who this is?

PEDRO

130Too well, sir.

HIERONIMO

Too well, sir. Too well, who? Who is it? Peace, Isabella!
131Nay, blush not, man.

PEDRO

Nay, blush not, man. It is my lord Horatio.

HIERONIMO

132Ha, ha! Saint James, but this doth make me laugh,
133That there are more deluded than myself.

PEDRO

134Deluded?

HIERONIMO

Deluded? Ay:
135I would have sworn myself, within this hour,
136That this had been my son Horatio,
137His garments are so like.
138Ha! are they not great persuasions?

ISABELLA

139O, would to God it were not so!

HIERONIMO

140Were not, Isabella? Dost thou dream it is?
141Can thy soft bosom entertain a thought,
142That such a black deed of mischief should be done
143On one so pure and spotless as our son?
144Away, I am ashamèd.

ISABELLA

Away, I am ashamèd. Dear Hieronimo,
145Cast a more serious eye upon thy grief:
146Weak apprehension gives but weak belief.

HIERONIMO

147It was a man, sure, that was hanged up here;
148A youth, as I remember: I cut him down.
149If it should prove my son now after all —
150Say you? say you? — Light! Lend me a taper;
151Let me look again. —O God!
152Confusion, mischief, torment, death and hell,
153Drop all your stings at once in my cold bosom,
154That now is stiff with horror: Kill me quickly!
155Be gracious to me, thou infective night,
156And drop this deed of murder down on me;
157Gird in my waste of grief with thy large darkness,
158And let me not survive to see the light
159May put me in the mind I had a son.

ISABELLA

160O sweet Horatio! O my dearest son!

HIERONIMO

161How strangely had I lost my way to grief! </sup> Q4 <sup>
162Sweet lovely rose, ill-pluck’d before thy time,
163Fair worthy son, not conquer’d but betray’d,
164I’ll kiss thee now, for words with tears are stay’d.

ISABELLA

165And I’ll close up the glasses of his sight,
166For once these eyes were only my delight.

HIERONIMO

167See’st thou this handkerchief besmear’d with blood?
168It shall not from me, till I take revenge.
169See’st thou those wounds that yet are bleeding fresh?
170I’ll not entomb them, till I have reveng’d.
171Then will I joy amidst my discontent;
172Till then my sorrow never shall be spent.

ISABELLA

173The heavens are just; murder cannot be hid:
174Time is the author both of truth and right,
175And time will bring this treachery to light.

HIERONIMO

176Meanwhile, good Isabella, cease thy plaints,
177Or, at the least, dissemble them a while:
178So shall we sooner find the practice out,
179And learn by whom all this was brought about.
180Come, Isabel, now let us take him up,

They take him up.

181And bear him in from out this cursèd place.
182I’ll say his dirge; singing fits not this case.
183O aliquis mihi quas pulchrum ver educat herbas

Hieronimo sets his breast unto his sword.

184Misceat, et nostro detur medicina dolori;
185Aut, si qui faciunt annorum oblivia, succos
186Praebeat; ipse metam magnum quaecunque per orbem
187Gramina Sol pulchras effert in luminis oras;
188Ipse bibam quicquid meditatur saga veneni,
189Quicquid et herbarum vi caeca nenia nectit:
190Omnia perpetiar, lethum quoque, dum semel omnis
191Noster in extincto moriatur pectore sensus.—
192Ergo tuos oculos nunquam, mea vita, videbo,
193Et tua perpetuus sepelivit lumina somnus?
194Emoriar tecum: sic, sic juvat ire sub umbras.—
195At tamen absistam properato cedere letho,
196Ne mortem vindicta tuam tum nulla sequatur.

Here he throws it from him and bears the body away.

[SCENE V]

Ghost of ANDREA, REVENGE.

ANDREA

1Brought’st thou me hither to increase my pain?
2I look’d that Balthazar should have been slain:
3But ’tis my friend Horatio that is slain,
4And they abuse fair Bel-imperia,
5On whom I doted more than all the world,
6Because she lov’d me more than all the world.

REVENGE

7Thou talk’st of harvest when the corn is green:
8The end is crown of every work well done;
9The sickle comes not till the corn be ripe.
10Be still, and ere I lead thee from this place,
11I’ll show thee Balthazar in heavy case.

Act III

[SCENE I]

Enter VICEROY OF PORTINGALE, NOBLES, VILLUPPO.

VICEROY

1Infortunate condition of kings,
2Seated amidst so many helpless doubts!
3First we are plac’d upon extremest height,
4And oft supplanted with exceeding heat,
5But ever subject to the wheel of Chance;
6And at our highest never joy we so,
7As we both doubt and dread our overthrow.
8So striveth not the waves with sundry winds,
9As Fortune toileth in the affairs of kings,
10That would be fear’d, yet fear to be belov’d,
11Sith fear or love to kings is flattery.
12For instance, lordings, look upon your King,
13By hate deprivèd of his dearest son,
14The only hope of our successive line.

NOBLEMAN

15I had no t thought that Alexandro’s heart
16Had been envenom’d with such extreme hate;
17But now I see that words have several works,
18And there’s no credit in the countenance.

VILLUPPO

19No: for, my lord, had you beheld the train
20That feignèd love had coloured in his looks,
21When he in camp consorted Balthazar,
22Far more inconstant had you thought the sun,
23That hourly coasts the centre of the earth,
24Than Alexandro’s purpose to the Prince.

VICEROY

25No more, Villuppo, thou hast said enough,
26And with thy words thou slay’st our wounded thoughts.
27Nor shall I longer dally with the world,
28Procrastinating Alexandro’s death:
29Go some of you, and fetch the traitor forth,
30That, as he is condemnèd, he may die.

Enter ALEXANDRO with a NOBLEMAN and Halberts.

NOBLEMAN

31In such extremes will naught but patience serve.

ALEXANDRO

32But in extremes, what patience shall I use?
33Nor discontents it me to leave the world,
34With whom there nothing can prevail but wrong.

NOBLEMAN

35Yet hope the best.

ALEXANDRO

Yet hope the best. ’Tis Heaven is my hope:
36As for the earth, it is too much infect
37To yield me hope of any of her mould.

VICEROY

38Why linger ye? Bring forth that daring fiend,
39And let him die for his accursèd deed.

ALEXANDRO

40Not that I fear the extremity of death
41(For nobles cannot stoop to servile fear)
42Do I, O King, thus discontented live.
43But this, O this, torments my labouring soul,
44That thus I die suspected of a sin
45Whereof, as heav’ns have known my secret thoughts,
46So am I free from this suggestion.

VICEROY

47No more, I say! To the tortures! When?
48Bind him, and burn his body in those flames,

They bind him to the stake.

49That shall prefigure those unquenchèd fires
50Of Phlegethon, prepared for his soul.

ALEXANDRO

51My guiltless death will be aveng’d on thee,
52On thee, Villuppo, that hath malic’d thus,
53Or for thy meed hast falsely me accus’d.

VILLUPPO

54Nay, Alexandro, if thou menace me,
55I’ll lend a hand to send thee to the lake,
56Where those thy words shall perish with thy works:
57Injurious traitor! monstrous homicide!

Enter AMBASSADOR [and Attendants].

AMBASSADOR

58Stay, hold a while;
59And here —with pardon of his majesty —
60Lay hands upon Villuppo.

VICEROY

Lay hands upon Villuppo. Ambassador,
61What news hath urg’d this sudden entrance?

AMBASSADOR

62Know, sovereign lord, that Balthazar doth live.

VICEROY

63What say’st thou? Liveth Balthazar our son?

AMBASSADOR

64Your highness’ son, lord Balthazar, doth live;
65And, well entreated in the court of Spain,
66Humbly commends him to your majesty.
67These eyes beheld; and these my followers,
68With these, the letters of the King’s commends,

Gives him letters

69Are happy witnesses of his highness’ health.

The Viceroy looks on the letters, and proceeds.

VICEROY

70“Thy son doth live, your tribute is receiv’d;
71The peace is made and we are satisfied.
72The rest resolve upon as things propos’d
73For both our honours and thy benefit.”

AMBASSADOR

74These are his highness’ farther articles.

He gives him more letters.

VICEROY

75Accursèd wretch, to intimate these ills
76Against the life and reputation
77Of noble Alexandro! Come, my lord,

[Unbind him.]

78Let him unbind thee, that is bound to death,
79To make a quittal for thy discontent.

They unbind him.

ALEXANDRO

80Dread lord, in kindness you could do no less,
81Upon report of such a damnèd fact;
82But thus we see our innocence hath sav’d
83The hopeless life which thou, Villuppo, sought
84By thy suggestions to have massacred.

VICEROY

85Say, false Villuppo, wherefore didst thou thus
86Falsely betray lord Alexandro’s life?
87Him whom thou know’st that no unkindness else
88But ev’n the slaughter of our dearest son
89Could once have mov’d us to have misconceiv’d.

ALEXANDRO

90Say, treacherous Villuppo, tell the King:
91Wherein hath Alexandro us’d thee ill?

VILLUPPO

92Rent with remembrance of so foul a deed,
93My guilty soul submits me to thy doom:
94For, not for Alexandro’s injuries,
95But for reward and hope to be preferr’d,
96Thus have I shamelessly hazarded his life.

VICEROY

97Which, villain, shall be ransom’d with thy death,
98And not so mean a torment as we here
99Devis’d for him who thou said’st, slew our son,
100But with the bitterest torments and extremes
101That may be yet invented for thine end.

Alexandro seems to entreat.

102Entreat me not! go, take the traitor hence:

Exit Villuppo [guarded].

103And, Alexandro, let us honour thee
104With public notice of thy loyalty. —
105To end those things articulated here
106By our great lord the mighty King of Spain,
107We with our council will deliberate.
108Come, Alexandro, keep us company.

Exeunt.

[SCENE II]

Enter HIERONIMO.

HIERONIMO

1O eyes! no eyes, but fountains fraught with tears;
2O life! no life, but lively form of death;
3O world! no world, but mass of public wrongs,
4Confus’d and fill’d with murder and misdeeds!
5O sacred heavens, if this unhallow’d deed,
6If this inhuman and barbarous attempt,
7If this incomparable murder thus
8Of [son of] mine, but now no more my son,
9Shall unreveal’d and unrevenged pass,
10How should we term your dealings to be just,
11If you unjustly deal with those that in your justice trust?
12The night, sad secretary to my moans,
13With direful visions wake my vexèd soul,
14And with the wounds of my distressful son
15Solicits me for notice of his death.
16The ugly fiends do sally forth of hell,
17And frame my steps to unfrequented paths,
18And fear my heart with fierce inflamèd thoughts.
19The cloudy day my discontents records,
20Early begins to register my dreams,
21And drive me forth to seek the murderer.
22Eyes, life, world, heav’ns, hell, night and day,
23See, search, shew, send some man, some mean that may —

A letter falleth.

24What’s here? A letter? Tush! it is not so! —
25A letter written to Hieronimo!

Red ink.

26“For want of ink, receive this bloody writ:
27Me hath my hapless brother hid from thee;
28Revenge thyself on Balthazar and him,
29For these were they that murderèd thy son.
30Hieronimo, revenge Horatio’s death,
31And better fare than Bel-imperia doth.”
32What means this unexpected miracle?
33My son slain by Lorenzo and the prince!
34What cause had they Horatio to malign?
35Or what might move thee, Bel-imperia,
36To accuse thy brother, had he been the mean?
37Hieronimo, beware! thou art betray’d,
38And to entrap thy life this train is laid.
39Advise thee therefore, be not credulous:
40This is devisèd to endanger thee,
41That thou, by this, Lorenzo shouldst accuse,
42And he, for thy dishonour done, should draw
43Thy life in question and thy name in hate.
44Dear was the life of my belovèd son,
45And of his death behoves me be reveng’d:
46Then hazard not thine own, Hieronimo,
47But live t’effect thy resolution.
48I therefore will by circumstances try,
49What I can gather to confirm this writ;
50And, heark’ning near the Duke of Castile’s house,
51Close, if I can, with Bel-imperia,
52To listen more, but nothing to bewray.

Enter PEDRINGANO.

53Now, Pedringano!

PEDRINGANO

Now, Pedringano! Now, Hieronimo!

HIERONIMO

54Where’s thy lady?

PEDRINGANO

Where’s thy lady? I know not; here’s my lord.

Enter LORENZO.

LORENZO

55How now, who’s this? Hieronimo?

HIERONIMO

How now, who’s this? Hieronimo? My lord!

PEDRINGANO

56He asketh for my lady Bel-imperia.

LORENZO

57What to do, Hieronimo? The Duke, my father, hath,
58Upon some disgrace awhile remov’d her hence;
59But if it be aught I may inform her of,
60Tell me, Hieronimo, and I’ll let her know it.

HIERONIMO

61Nay, nay, my lord, I thank you; it shall not need.
62I had a suit unto her, but too late,
63And her disgrace makes me unfortunate.

LORENZO

64Why so, Hieronimo? Use me.

HIERONIMO

65Oh no, my lord; I dare not; it must not be;
66I humbly thank your lordship.

HIERONIMO

67<sup> Q4 </sup> Who? you, my lord?
68I reserve your favour for a greater honour;
69This is a very toy, my lord, a toy.

LORENZO

70All’s one, Hieronimo, acquaint me with it.

HIERONIMO

71I’faith, my lord, it is an idle thing;
72I must confess I ha’ been too slack, too tardy,
73Too remiss unto your honour.

LORENZO

74How now, Hieronimo?

HIERONIMO

75In troth, my lord, it is a thing of nothing:
76The murder of a son, or so —
77A thing of nothing, my lord! </sup> Q4 <sup>

LORENZO

78Why then, farewell.

HIERONIMO

79My grief no heart, my thoughts no tongue can tell.

Exit.

LORENZO

80Come hither, Pedringano, see’st thou this?

PEDRINGANO

81My lord, I see it, and suspect it too.

LORENZO

82This is that damned villain Serberine,
83That hath, I fear, reveal’d Horatio’s death.

PEDRINGANO

84My lord, he could not, ’twas so lately done;
85And since, he hath not left my company.

LORENZO

86Admit he have not, his condition’s such,
87As fear or flattering words may make him false.
88I know his humour, and therewith repent
89That e’er I us’d him in this enterprise.
90But, Pedringano, to prevent the worst,
91And ’cause I know thee secret as my soul,
92Here, for thy further satisfaction, take thou this.

Gives him more gold.

93And hearken to me —thus it is devis’d:
94This night thou must (and, prithee, so resolve)
95Meet Serberine at Saint Luigi’s park —
96Thou know’st ’tis here hard by behind the house —
97There take thy stand, and see thou strike him sure:
98For die he must, if we do mean to live.

PEDRINGANO

99But how shall Serberine be there, my lord?

LORENZO

100Let me alone; I’ll send to him to meet
101The prince and me, where thou must do this deed.

PEDRINGANO

102It shall be done, my lord, it shall be done;
103And I’ll go arm myself to meet him there.

LORENZO

104When things shall alter, as I hope they will,
105Then shalt thou mount for this; thou know’st my mind.

Exit Pedringano.

106Chi l’è? Jeron!

Enter PAGE.

PAGE

Chi l’è? Jeron! My lord?

LORENZO

Chi l’è? Jeron! My lord? Go, sirrah, to Serberine,
107And bid him forthwith meet the Prince and me
108At Saint Luigi’s park, behind the house;
109This evening, boy!

PAGE

This evening, boy! I go, my lord.

LORENZO

110But sirrah, let the hour be eight o’clock:
111Bid him not fail.

PAGE

Bid him not fail. I fly, my lord.

Exit.

LORENZO

112Now, to confirm the complot thou hast cast
113Of all these practices, I’ll spread the watch,
114Upon precise commandment from the King,
115Strongly to guard the place where Pedringano
116This night shall murder hapless Serberine.
117Thus must we work that will avoid distrust;
118Thus must we practise to prevent mishap,
119And thus one ill another must expulse.
120This sly enquiry of Hieronimo
121For Bel-imperia breeds suspicion,
122And this suspicion bodes a further ill.
123As for myself, I know my secret fault,
124And so do they; but I have dealt for them:
125They that for coin their souls endangerèd,
126To save my life, for coin shall venture theirs;
127And better ’tis that base companions die,
128Than by their life to hazard our good haps.
129Nor shall they live for me to fear their faith:
130I’ll trust myself, myself shall be my friend;
131For die they shall, slaves are ordain’d to no other end.

Exit.

[SCENE III]

Enter PEDRINGANO with a pistol.

PEDRINGANO

1Now, Pedringano, bid thy pistol hold,
2And hold on, Fortune! once more favour me;
3Give but success to mine attempting spirit,
4And let me shift for taking of mine aim.
5Here is the gold: this is the gold propos’d;
6It is no dream that I adventure for,
7But Pedringano is possess’d thereof.
8And he that would not strain his conscience
9For him that thus his liberal purse hath stretch’d,
10Unworthy such a favour, may he fail,
11And, wishing, want, when such as I prevail.
12As for the fear of apprehension,
13I know, if need should be, my noble lord
14Will stand between me and ensuing harms;
15Besides, this place is free from all suspect:
16Here therefore will I stay and take my stand.

Enter the WATCH.

1 WATCH

17I wonder much to what intent it is
18That we are thus expressly charg’d to watch.

2 WATCH

19’Tis by commandment in the King’s own name.

3 WATCH

20But we were never wont to watch and ward
21So near the duke, his brother’s house before.

2 WATCH

22Content yourself, stand close, there’s somewhat in’t.

Enter SERBERINE.

SERBERINE

23Here, Serberine, attend and stay thy pace;
24For here did Don Lorenzo’s page appoint
25That thou by his command shouldst meet with him.
26How fit a place, if one were so dispos’d,
27Methinks this corner is to close with one.

PEDRINGANO

28Here comes the bird that I must seize upon:
29Now, Pedringano, or never, play the man!

SERBERINE

30I wonder that his lordship stays so long,
31Or wherefore should he send for me so late?

PEDRINGANO

32For this, Serberine! — and thou shalt ha’t.

Shoots the dag.

33So, there he lies; my promise is perform’d.

The Watch.

1 WATCH

34Hark, gentlemen, this is a pistol shot.

2 WATCH

35And here’s one slain; —Stay the murderer.

PEDRINGANO

36Now by the sorrows of the souls in hell,

He strives with the Watch.

37Who first lays hand on me, I’ll be his priest.

3 WATCH

38Sirrah, confess, and therein play the priest,
39Why hast thou thus unkindly kill’d the man?

PEDRINGANO

40Why? because he walk’d abroad so late.

3 WATCH

41Come, sir, you had been better kept your bed,
42Than have committed this misdeed so late.

2 WATCH

43Come, to the Marshal’s with the murderer!

1 WATCH

44On to Hieronimo’s! help me here
45To bring the murder’d body with us too.

PEDRINGANO

46Hieronimo? carry me before whom you will:
47Whate’er he be, I’ll answer him and you;
48And do your worst, for I defy you all.

Exeunt.

[SCENE IV]

Enter LORENZO and BALTHAZAR.

BALTHAZAR

1How now, my lord, what makes you rise so soon?

LORENZO

2Fear of preventing our mishaps too late.

BALTHAZAR

3What mischief is it that we not mistrust?

LORENZO

4Our greatest ills we least mistrust, my lord,
5And inexpected harms do hurt us most.

BALTHAZAR

6Why, tell me, Don Lorenzo, tell me, man,
7If ought concerns our honour and your own.

LORENZO

8Nor you, nor me, my lord, but both in one:
9For I suspect, and the presumption’s great,
10That, by those base confederates in our fault
11Touching the death of Don Horatio,
12We are betray’d to old Hieronimo.

BALTHAZAR

13Betray’d, Lorenzo? Tush! it cannot be.

LORENZO

14A guilty conscience, urged with the thought
15Of former evils, easily cannot err:
16I am persuaded, and dissuade me not,
17That all’s revealèd to Hieronimo.
18And therefore know that I have cast it thus: —

[Enter PAGE.]

19But here’s the page. How now? what news with thee?

PAGE

20My lord, Serberine is slain.

BALTHAZAR

21Who? Serberine, my man?

PAGE

22Your highness’ man, my lord.

LORENZO

23Speak, page, who murder’d him?

PAGE

24He that is apprehended for the fact.

LORENZO

25Who?

PAGE

26Pedringano.

BALTHAZAR

27Is Serberine slain that lov’d his lord so well?
28Injurious villain, murderer of his friend!

LORENZO

29Hath Pedringano murder’d Serberine?
30My lord, let me entreat you to take the pains
31To exasperate and hasten his revenge
32With your complaints unto my lord the King.
33This their dissension breeds a greater doubt.

BALTHAZAR

34Assure thee, Don Lorenzo, he shall die,
35Or else his highness hardly shall deny.
36Meanwhile, I’ll haste the marshal-sessions:
37For die he shall for this his damnèd deed.

Exit Balthazar.

LORENZO

38Why so, this fits our former policy,
39And thus experience bids the wise to deal.
40I lay the plot: he prosecutes the point;
41I set the trap: he breaks the worthless twigs,
42And sees not that wherewith the bird was lim’d.
43Thus hopeful men, that mean to hold their own,
44Must look like fowlers to their dearest friends.
45He runs to kill whom I have holp to catch,
46And no man knows it was my reaching fatch.
47’Tis hard to trust unto a multitude,
48Or any one, in mine opinion,
49When men themselves their secrets will reveal.

Enter a MESSENGER with a letter.

50Boy!

PAGE

Boy! My lord.

LORENZO

51What’s he?

MESSENGER

What’s he? I have a letter to your lordship.

LORENZO

52From whence?

MESSENGER

From whence? From Pedringano that’s imprison’d.

LORENZO

53So, he is in prison then?

MESSENGER

So, he is in prison then? Ay, my good lord.

LORENZO

54What would he with us? —He writes us here,
55To stand good, lord and help him in distress.
56Tell him I have his letters, know his mind,
57And what we may, let him assure him of.
58Fellow, begone; my boy shall follow thee.

Exit Messenger.

59This works like wax, yet once more try thy wits.
60Boy, go, convey this purse to Pedringano;
61Thou know’st the prison, closely give it him,
62And be advis’d that none be there about:
63Bid him be merry still, but secret;
64And, though the marshal-sessions be to-day,
65Bid him not doubt of his delivery.
66Tell him his pardon is already sign’d,
67And thereon bid him boldly be resolv’d,
68For, were he ready to be turnèd off —
69As ’tis my will the uttermost be tried —
70Thou with his pardon shalt attend him still.
71Show him this box, tell him his pardon’s in’t;
72But open’t not, an if thou lovest thy life;
73But let him wisely keep his hopes unknown.
74He shall not want while Don Lorenzo lives.
75Away!

PAGE

Away! I go, my lord, I run.

LORENZO

76But, sirrah, see that this be cleanly done.

Exit Page.

77Now stands our fortune on a tickle point,
78And now or never ends Lorenzo’s doubts.
79One only thing is uneffected yet,
80And that’s to see the executioner.
81But to what end? I list not trust the air
82With utterance of our pretence therein,
83For fear the privy whisp’ring of the wind
84Convey our words amongst unfriendly ears
85That lie too open to advantages.
86E quel che voglio io, nessun lo sa,
87Intendo io; quel mi basterà.

Exit.

[SCENE V]

Enter Boy, with the box.

BOY

My master hath forbidden me to look in this box; and, by
my troth, ’tis likely, if he had not warned me, I should not
have had so much idle time; for we men’s-kind in our
minority, are like women in their uncertainty: that they
are most forbidden, they will soonest attempt: so I now.
—By my bare honesty, here’s nothing but the bare
empty box: were it not sin against secrecy, I would say it
were a piece of gentlemanlike knavery. I must go to
Pedringano, and tell him his pardon is in this box: nay, I
would have sworn it, had I not seen the contrary. I cannot
choose but smile to think how the villain will flout the
gallows, scorn the audience and descant on the hangman,
and all presuming of his pardon from hence. Will’t not be
an odd jest for me to stand and grace every jest he makes,
pointing my finger at this box, as who would say: “Mock
on, here’s thy warrant.” Is’t not a scurvy jest that a man
should jest himself to death? Alas! Por Pedringano, I
am in a sort sorry for thee, but if I should be hanged with
thee, I cannot weep.

Exit.

[SCENE VI]

Enter HIERONIMO and the DEPUTY.

HIERONIMO

1Thus must we toil in other men’s extremes,
2That know not how to remedy our own;
3And do them justice, when unjustly we,
4For all our wrongs, can compass no redress.
5But shall I never live to see the day,
6That I may come, by justice of the heavens,
7To know the cause that may my cares allay?
8This toils my body, this consumeth age,
9That only I to all men just must be,
10And neither gods nor men be just to me.

DEPUTY

11Worthy Hieronimo, your office asks
12A care to punish such as do transgress.

HIERONIMO

13So is’t my duty to regard his death
14Who, when he liv’d, deserv’d my dearest blood.
15But come, for that we came for: let’s begin;
16For here lies that which bids me to be gone.

Enter Officers, Boy, and PEDRINGANO, with a letter in his hand, bound.

DEPUTY

17Bring forth the prisoner, for the court is set.

PEDRINGANO

18Gramercy, boy, but it was time to come;
19For I had written to my lord anew
20A nearer matter that concerneth him,
21For fear his lordship had forgotten me.
22But sith he hath remember’d me so well —
23Come, come, come on, when shall we to this gear?

HIERONIMO

24Stand forth, thou monster, murderer of men,
25And here, for satisfaction of the world,
26Confess thy folly, and repent thy fault;
27For there’s thy place of execution.

PEDRINGANO

28This is short work: Well, to your marshalship
29First I confess —nor fear I death therefore —
30I am the man, ’twas I slew Serberine.
31But, sir, then you think this shall be the place
32Where we shall satisfy you for this gear?

DEPUTY

33Ay, Pedringano.

PEDRINGANO

Ay, Pedringano. Now I think not so.

HIERONIMO

34Peace, impudent, for thou shalt find it so.
35For blood with blood shall, while I sit as judge,
36Be satisfied, and the law discharg’d.
37And though myself cannot receive the like,
38Yet will I see that others have their right.
39Despatch: the fault’s approvèd and confess’d,
40And by our law he is condemn’d to die.

HANGMAN

Come on, sir, are you ready?

PEDRINGANO

To do what, my fine officious knave?

HANGMAN

To go to this gear.

PEDRINGANO

O sir, you are too forward: thou wouldst fain furnish me
with a halter to disfurnish me of my habit. So I should
go out of this gear, my raiment, into that gear, the rope.
But, hangman, now I spy your knavery, I’ll not change
without boot, that’s flat.

HANGMAN

Come, sir.

PEDRINGANO

So, then, I must up?

HANGMAN

No remedy.

PEDRINGANO

Yes, but there shall be for my coming down.

HANGMAN

Indeed, here’s a remedy for that.

PEDRINGANO

How? be turned off?

HANGMAN

Ay, truly; come, are you ready? I pray, sir, despatch;
the day goes away.

PEDRINGANO

What, do you hang by the hour? If you do, I may chance
to break your old custom.

HANGMAN

Faith, you have reason; for I am like to break your
young neck.

PEDRINGANO

Dost thou mock me, hangman? Pray God, I be not preserved
to break your knave’s pate for this.

HANGMAN

Alas, sir! you are a foot too low to reach it, and I hope
you will never grow so high while I am in the office.

PEDRINGANO

Sirrah, dost see yonder boy with the box in his hand?

HANGMAN

What, he that points to it with his finger?

PEDRINGANO

Ay, that companion.

HANGMAN

I know him not; but what of him?

PEDRINGANO

Dost thou think to live till his old doublet will make thee
a new truss?

HANGMAN

Ay, and many a fair year after, to truss up many a
honester man than either thou or he.

PEDRINGANO

What hath he in his box, as thou thinkest?

HANGMAN

Faith, I cannot tell, nor I care not greatly; Methinks
you should rather hearken to your soul’s health.

PEDRINGANO

Why, sirrah hangman, I take it that that is good for
the body is likewise good for the soul; and, it may be, in that
box is balm for both.

HANGMAN

Well, thou art even the merriest piece of man’s flesh
that e’er groaned at my office door.

PEDRINGANO

Is your roguery become an office with a knave’s name?

HANGMAN

Ay, and that shall all they witness that see you seal it
with a thief’s name.

PEDRINGANO

I prithee, request this good company to pray with me.

HANGMAN

Ay, marry, sir, this is a good motion: my masters, you
see here’s a good fellow —

PEDRINGANO

Nay, nay, now I remember me, let them alone till some
other time; for now I have no great need.

HIERONIMO

89I have not seen a wretch so impudent.
90Oh, monstrous times where murder’s set so light,
91And where the soul, that should be shrin’d in heaven,
92Solely delights in interdicted things,
93Still wand’ring in the thorny passages,
94That intercepts itself of happiness.
95Murder! O bloody monster! God forbid
96A fault so foul should ’scape unpunishèd.
97Despatch, and see this execution done! —
98This makes me to remember thee, my son.

Exit Hieronimo.

PEDRINGANO

Nay, soft, no haste.

DEPUTY

Why, wherefore stay you? Have you hope of life?

PEDRINGANO

Why, ay!

HANGMAN

As how?

PEDRINGANO

Why, rascal, by my pardon from the King.

HANGMAN

Stand you on that? Then you shall off with this.

He turns him off.

DEPUTY

105So, executioner; —convey him hence;
106But let his body be unburièd.
107Let not the earth be chokèd or infect
108With that which heaven contemns, and men neglect.

Exeunt.

[SCENE VII]

Enter HIERONIMO.

HIERONIMO

1Where shall I run to breathe abroad my woes,
2My woes whose weight hath wearièd the earth?
3Or mine exclaims, that have surchargèd the air
4With ceaseless plaints for my deceasèd son?
5The blust’ring winds, conspiring with my words,
6At my lament have mov’d the leafless trees,
7Disrob’d the meadows of their flower’d green,
8Made mountains marsh with spring-tides of my tears,
9And broken through the brazen gates of hell.
10Yet still tormented is my tortur’d soul
11With broken sighs and restless passions,
12That wingèd, mount; and, hovering in the air,
13Beat at the windows of the brightest heavens,
14Soliciting for justice and revenge:
15But they are plac’d in those empyreal heights,
16Where, countermur’d with walls of diamond,
17I find the place impregnable; and they
18Resist my woes, and give my words no way.

Enter HANGMAN with a letter.

HANGMAN

O lord, sir! God bless you, sir! the man, sir, Petergade,
sir, he that was so full of merry conceits —

HIERONIMO

Well, what of him?

HANGMAN

O Lord, sir, he went the wrong way; the fellow had a
fair commission to the contrary. Sir, here is his passport;
I pray you, sir, we have done him wrong.

HIERONIMO

I warrant thee, give it me.

HANGMAN

You will stand between the gallows and me?

HIERONIMO

Ay, ay.

HANGMAN

I thank your lord worship.

Exit Hangman.

HIERONIMO

29And yet, though somewhat nearer me concerns,
30I will, to ease the grief that I sustain,
31Take truce with sorrow while I read on this.
32“My lord, I writ, as mine extremes requirèd,
33That you would labour my delivery:
34If you neglect, my life is desperate,
35And in my death I shall reveal the truth.
36You know, my lord, I slew him for your sake,
37And was confederate with the prince and you,
38Won by rewards and hopeful promises,
39I holp to murder Don Horatio too.” —
40Holp he to murder mine Horatio?
41And actors in th’accursèd tragedy
42Wast thou Lorenzo, Balthazar, and thou,
43Of whom my son, my son deserv’d so well?
44What have I heard? what have mine eyes beheld?
45O sacred heavens, may it come to pass
46That such a monstrous and detested deed,
47So closely smother’d and so long conceal’d,
48Shall thus by this be vengèd or reveal’d?
49Now see I what I durst not then suspect,
50That Bel-imperia’s letter was not feign’d,
51Nor feignèd she, though falsely they have wrong’d
52Both her, myself, Horatio, and themselves.
53Now may I make compare ’twixt hers and this,
54Of every accident; I ne’er could find
55Till now, and now I feelingly perceive
56They did what heaven unpunish’d would not leave.
57O false Lorenzo! are these thy flatt’ring looks?
58Is this the honour that thou didst my son?
59And Balthazar —bane to thy soul and me! —
60Was this the ransom he reserv’d thee for?
61Woe to the cause of these constrainèd wars!
62Woe to thy baseness and captivity,
63Woe to thy birth, thy body, and thy soul,
64Thy cursèd father, and thy conquer’d self!
65And bann’d with bitter execrations be
66The day and place where he did pity thee!
67But wherefore waste I mine unfruitful words,
68When naught but blood will satisfy my woes?
69I will go plain me to my lord the King,
70And cry aloud for justice through the court,
71Wearing the flints with these my wither’d feet,
72And either purchase justice by entreats,
73Or tire them all with my revenging threats.

Exit.

[SCENE VIII]

Enter ISABELLA and her MAID.

ISABELLA

1So that, you say, this herb will purge the eye,
2And this, the head? —
3Ah, but none of them will purge the heart!
4No, there’s no medicine left for my disease,
5Nor any physic to recure the dead.

She runs lunatic

6Horatio! Oh, where’s Horatio?

MAID

7Good madam, affright not thus yourself
8With outrage for your son Horatio:
9He sleeps in quiet in the Elysian fields.

ISABELLA

10Why, did I not give you gowns and goodly things,
11Bought you a whistle and a whipstock too,
12To be revengèd on their villainies?

MAID

13Madam, these humours do torment my soul.

ISABELLA

14My soul! —poor soul! thou talks of things
15Thou know’st not what. My soul hath silver wings,
16That mounts me up unto the highest heavens;
17To heav’n: ay, there sits my Horatio,
18Backed with a troop of fiery Cherubins
19Dancing about his newly healed wounds,
20Singing sweet hymns and chanting heavenly notes:
21Rare harmony to greet his innocence,
22That died, ay died, a mirror in our days.
23But say, where shall I find the men, the murderers,
24That slew Horatio? Whither shall I run
25To find them out that murdered my son?

Exeunt.

[SCENE IX]
